questions.q: Which term describes the study of how to crack encryption algorithms or their implementations?

choices.why: Correct. Cryptanalysis is the study of how to break encryption algorithms or the way they are implemented.
Cryptography (cryptology) is the study of techniques for encryption and secure communications, not specifically of breaking them.
Key management covers generating, verifying, exchanging, storing, and destroying keys, not cracking algorithms.
Steganalysis is detecting hidden data inside other content; the term for cracking encryption algorithms is cryptanalysis.

questions.q: An engineer wants a symmetric cipher that encrypts plaintext one bit at a time against a key stream and never needs padding. Which cipher type fits?

choices.why: A block cipher works on fixed-size groups of bits and adds padding when there is not enough data to fill a block.
Correct. A stream cipher encrypts one bit at a time against the key stream, needs no padding, and so has slightly less overhead than a block cipher.
A transposition cipher rearranges the letters of the message; it does not combine bits with a key stream.
An asymmetric cipher uses a public and private key pair; stream and block ciphers are both symmetric.

questions.q: Which port and protocol does IKE (ISAKMP) use for IPsec key negotiation?

choices.why: UDP 4500 is used by NAT Traversal (NAT-T) to carry IPsec through NAT devices, not for normal IKE negotiation.
TCP 443 is HTTPS, which is HTTP combined with TLS/SSL.
Correct. IKE (ISAKMP) negotiates IPsec keys over UDP 500.
UDP 123 is NTP, which keeps clocks correct so certificate validity dates are not misread.

questions.q: How is a digital signature created?

choices.text: The data is encrypted with the receiver's public key
choices.why: Encrypting with the receiver's public key provides confidentiality (as in PGP email), not a signature that proves who sent the data.

choices.text: A hash is encrypted with the receiver's private key
choices.why: The sender never has the receiver's private key; a private key is known only to its owner.

choices.text: The data is hashed with a shared secret key
choices.why: Hashing with a shared secret key produces an HMAC, which gives integrity but not nonrepudiation.

choices.text: A hash is encrypted with the sender's private key
choices.why: Correct. The sender hashes the data and encrypts that hash with its own private key, then attaches the result to the data.

questions.q: What is the digest length of SHA-1?

choices.why: 128 bits is the digest length of MD5, which is broken and should be avoided.
Correct. SHA-1 produces a 160-bit hash; it is outdated and has known vulnerabilities.
224 bits is the smallest SHA-2 or SHA-3 output size, not SHA-1.
512 bits is the size of Whirlpool and SHA-512, not SHA-1.

questions.q: On a root certificate, which entity appears in the Subject field?

choices.why: Correct. A root certificate identifies the CA and holds the CA's public key, so its subject is the CA.

choices.text: The web server that requested it
choices.why: A web server or router is the subject of an identity certificate, not of a root certificate.
A subordinate CA is the subject of its own certificate signed by the root, not of the root certificate.

choices.text: The LDAP server that publishes the CRL
choices.why: An LDAP server may host the CRL, but it is not the subject of the root certificate.

questions.q: A firewall must check whether a single peer certificate has been revoked without downloading and processing the CA's entire revocation list. Which method should it use?

choices.why: SCEP automates requesting and installing certificates; it is one way to reach a CRL but it is not a per-certificate status query.
A CRL is the full list of revoked serial numbers, which can be large and must be processed as a whole.
PKCS #10 is the format of a certificate request sent to a CA, not a revocation check.
Correct. OCSP asks for the status of one certificate instead of downloading the whole CRL.

questions.q: Which PKCS standard defines the certificate request a client sends to a CA, including the requester's public key?

choices.why: PKCS #7 is the CA's response to a request, usually containing the identity certificate.
PKCS #12 stores both public and private keys protected by a password-based symmetric key.
Correct. PKCS #10 is the certificate request sent to a CA, and it includes the requester's public key.
PKCS #1 is the RSA cryptography standard.

questions.q: Which CRYSTALS algorithm is a key-encapsulation mechanism (KEM)?

choices.why: Dilithium is the CRYSTALS digital signature algorithm, not the KEM.
Classic McEliece is a separate post-quantum algorithm and is not part of the CRYSTALS suite.
Correct. Kyber is the CRYSTALS key-encapsulation mechanism and is secure against chosen-ciphertext attacks (IND-CCA2).
ECDH is the elliptic curve Diffie-Hellman key exchange used in NGE; it is a classical algorithm, not part of CRYSTALS.

questions.q: Which Cisco IOS command verifies the integrity of a downloaded software image?

choices.why: md5sum is a Linux command that prints the MD5 checksum of files, not a Cisco IOS command.
shasum is a Linux/macOS command that prints SHA checksums of files, not a Cisco IOS command.
This command displays installed PKI certificates; it does not verify a software image hash.
Correct. The IOS verify md5 command checks a downloaded image's hash to confirm its integrity.

questions.q: A site-to-site IPsec VPN must provide encryption of the traffic. Which IPsec method must be used?

choices.why: Correct. ESP can do all IPsec features, including encryption.
AH provides most IPsec features but not encryption, which is why it is rarely used.
IKE handles negotiation and key management for IPsec; it is not the method that encapsulates and encrypts the data packets.
NAT-T lets IPsec pass through NAT using UDP 4500; it does not itself provide encryption.

questions.q: Which RFC defines TLS 1.3?

choices.why: RFC 5246 defined the older TLS 1.2; TLS 1.3 is defined in RFC 8446.
Correct. TLS 1.3, the latest version of TLS, is defined in RFC 8446.
RFC 2865 defines RADIUS, an AAA protocol, not TLS.
RFC 4301 describes the IPsec security architecture, not TLS 1.3.

questions.q: An administrator downloads a root CA certificate and then phones the CA's administrators to compare the certificate's hash. What is this practice called?

choices.why: Cross-certification is a horizontal trust relationship between two CAs, not a manual hash check.
Enrollment is requesting and receiving an identity certificate from a CA, which happens after the CA is authenticated.
Revocation invalidates a certificate before it expires, for example after a key compromise.
Correct. Checking the certificate's hash (thumbprint) through another channel, such as a phone call, is out-of-band verification.

questions.q: Which cipher method rearranges the letters of a message rather than replacing them?

choices.why: A substitution cipher replaces one character with another; it does not reorder them.
A polyalphabetic cipher substitutes characters using several alphabets, switching on a trigger character.
Correct. A transposition cipher rearranges the letters, such as writing the text in a grid and reading it back in a spiral.
A one-time pad combines each message bit with a pad bit of a single-use key the same length as the message.

questions.q: Diffie-Hellman is an asymmetric algorithm. What kind of keys does a DH exchange produce?

choices.text: A public and private key pair for each peer
choices.why: Key pairs are what asymmetric algorithms such as RSA use; DH's output is a shared secret, not a new key pair.

choices.text: Shared symmetric keys used with ciphers such as AES or 3DES
choices.why: Correct. DH lets two devices establish shared secret keying material over an untrusted network, and the resulting keys are symmetric.

choices.text: A digital certificate signed by a CA
choices.why: Certificates are issued and signed by a CA, not produced by a DH exchange.
A message digest is the output of a hash function such as SHA-2, not of DH.

questions.q: Suite B is approved by the U.S. government to protect classified information up to which levels?

choices.why: Correct. Suite B is the U.S. government's recommended set of standards, approved for classified information at the secret and top-secret levels.
Suite B is specifically approved for classified information, not limited to unclassified data.
Suite B approval covers secret and top-secret classified information, not only the confidential level.
Suite B reaches beyond unclassified data; it is approved for secret and top-secret information.

questions.q: What makes an HMAC different from a plain hash?

choices.text: It includes a secret key in the hash calculation
choices.why: Correct. An HMAC adds a secret key, so only someone with the key can create or verify the value, and an eavesdropper cannot recalculate it after changing data.

choices.text: It encrypts the hash with the sender's private key
choices.why: Encrypting a hash with a private key creates a digital signature, not an HMAC.
Hash and HMAC outputs are fixed length; the secret key is what sets an HMAC apart.

choices.text: It encrypts the entire payload with AES
choices.why: Encrypting the payload provides confidentiality; HMAC only provides integrity and authentication of the message.

questions.q: A company wants certificates for internal servers that only managed company devices will access and does not want to pay a fee. What is the trade-off of using an internal CA?

choices.text: Browsers on the internet will trust it automatically
choices.why: Automatic browser trust is the benefit of a commercial CA; an internal CA is not trusted outside the company.
An internal CA can issue standard X.509v3 certificates; the issue is trust, not format.

choices.text: Each device must be configured to trust the internal CA
choices.why: Correct. An internal CA is free, but you must configure each device to trust it, and it is only trusted inside the company.

choices.text: It cannot revoke certificates it issues
choices.why: An internal CA can publish CRLs and revoke certificates just like a commercial CA.

questions.q: Which series of directory service standards is the basis of Microsoft Active Directory?

choices.why: PKCS is a set of numbered Public Key Cryptography Standards for certificate formats and use, not directory services.
X.509 Version 3 is the standard for digital certificates; it uses X.500 naming but is not the directory standard itself.
LDAP is a protocol for directory lookups, not the series of standards that defines how directories are organized.
Correct. X.500 is the series of directory service standards and is the basis of Microsoft Active Directory.

questions.q: A router is being decommissioned, and its private key may have been copied. What should the PKI administrator do with its identity certificate?

choices.text: Renew it with a new validity date
choices.why: Renewing would keep a possibly compromised identity trusted; a decommissioned or compromised certificate should be revoked.

choices.text: Revoke it so its serial number is added to the CRL
choices.why: Correct. Certificates are revoked when a device is decommissioned or its private key is compromised, and the CRL lists them by serial number.
Cross-certification creates trust between two CAs; it does nothing to stop trust in one compromised certificate.
PKCS #12 is a format for storing public and private keys; exporting it would spread the key, not invalidate it.

questions.q: What does the term keyspace refer to?

choices.text: The storage area where private keys are kept
choices.why: Where keys are stored is part of key management; keyspace is about how many key values are possible.

choices.text: All possible values for a key
choices.why: Correct. Keyspace is every possible key value; a bigger key is more secure but uses more CPU.

choices.text: The number of keys a CA has issued
choices.why: A CA tracks issued certificates by serial number; that count is not the keyspace.

choices.text: The time a key remains valid
choices.why: A key's lifetime is handled by key management, which ends with destroying the key; keyspace is the set of possible values.

questions.q: Which statement correctly describes a one-time pad?

choices.text: It is a password that is valid for a single login
choices.why: That describes a one-time password, which the notes stress is not the same thing as a one-time pad.

choices.text: It is a short key reused for every message
choices.why: A one-time pad is used only once and must be as long as the message, so it is never a short reused key.

choices.text: It is a key used once and the same length as the message
choices.why: Correct. A one-time pad is used only once, matches the message length, and each pad bit is combined with a message bit; the receiver must also have the pad.

choices.text: It is a public key published on a key server
choices.why: Public keys are published for asymmetric cryptography such as PGP; a one-time pad is a secret shared only with the receiver.

questions.q: An IPsec VPN must encrypt a large volume of user traffic with low CPU impact. Which type of algorithm is best suited to the bulk data encryption?

choices.why: Asymmetric algorithms have a high CPU cost, so they are used sparingly for authentication and keying material, not bulk data.
A hash verifies integrity; it is one-way and does not encrypt data so it can be decrypted.

choices.text: Key exchange algorithm such as DH
choices.why: DH establishes shared keying material; the actual bulk encryption is done by a symmetric cipher using those keys.
Correct. Symmetric algorithms use the same key to encrypt and decrypt, are fast, and use little CPU, so they handle bulk data.

questions.q: ESP is identified by which value in the IP header?

choices.why: Correct. ESP is IP protocol 50 and has no port number.
IP protocol 51 is AH, the IPsec method that does not provide encryption.
UDP 500 is used by IKE (ISAKMP) for key negotiation, not by ESP data packets.
ESP is not carried over TCP and has no port; it is IP protocol 50.

questions.q: An MD5 hash is 128 bits long. How many hexadecimal digits are used to display it?

choices.why: 16 is the number of bytes in an MD5 hash; each byte takes two hex digits, so it displays as 32.
64 hex digits would represent 256 bits, such as a SHA-256 hash.
Correct. MD5 is 128 bits (16 bytes), shown as 32 hex digits.
128 hex digits is how a 512-bit SHA-512 hash is displayed.

questions.q: In next-generation encryption (NGE), which algorithm replaces RSA digital signatures?

choices.why: ECDH replaces DH key exchange in NGE, not RSA signatures.
Correct. ECDSA, the elliptic curve variant of DSA, replaces RSA signatures in NGE.
AES-GCM is the NGE mode for authenticated encryption, not a signature algorithm.
SHA-384 is an NGE hashing algorithm, not a digital signature algorithm.

questions.q: Which post-quantum algorithm is a digital signature scheme secure against existential forgery under adaptive chosen-message attacks (EUF-CMA)?

choices.why: Correct. Dilithium is the CRYSTALS digital signature algorithm and is EUF-CMA secure.
Kyber is the CRYSTALS key-encapsulation mechanism, secure against chosen-ciphertext attacks (IND-CCA2), not a signature scheme.
ElGamal is a classical asymmetric encryption system based on the DH exchange, not a post-quantum signature.
ECDSA is a classical elliptic curve signature used in NGE; it relies on math that quantum computers threaten.

questions.q: An administrator needs to move a device's certificate together with both its public and private keys to another server, protected by a password. Which format is designed for this?

choices.why: PKCS #10 is a certificate request that carries only the requester's public key.
PKCS #7 is the CA's response to a request, usually the identity certificate; it does not hold the private key.
PKCS #3 is the Diffie-Hellman key exchange standard.
Correct. PKCS #12 stores both public and private keys, protected by a symmetric password-based key.

questions.q: In a hierarchical PKI, what does a client need in order to verify another client's certificate chain?

choices.text: Only the other client's identity certificate
choices.why: The identity certificate alone cannot be trusted without verifying the CA signatures above it.

choices.text: The private key of the issuing subordinate CA
choices.why: A CA's private key is never shared; verification uses public keys inside the CA certificates.

choices.text: A cross-certification agreement with the root
choices.why: Cross-certification is horizontal trust between two separate CAs, not how a hierarchy is verified.

choices.text: Every certificate from the root down to the issuing CA
choices.why: Correct. To verify the chain, a client needs every certificate from the root CA down to the CA that issued the client's certificate.

questions.q: A laptop rejects a valid server certificate because its system clock is set to the wrong year. Which protocol should be used to prevent this?

choices.why: Correct. NTP (UDP 123) keeps clocks correct so certificate validity dates are not misread.
OCSP checks whether a certificate has been revoked; it does not fix the device's clock.
SCEP automates certificate requests and installation; it does not synchronize time.
LDAP is used for directory lookups and can deliver CRLs, but it does not keep clocks accurate.

questions.q: Why is a collision attack a serious threat to PKI?

choices.text: It reveals the CA's private key
choices.why: A collision attack targets the hash function, not the CA's private key directly.

choices.text: It undermines digital signatures and certificates
choices.why: Correct. If an attacker can create two inputs with the same hash, a signature over one can be passed off as valid for the other.

choices.text: It floods the CA with enrollment requests
choices.why: Flooding a CA would be a denial-of-service attack, not a collision attack.
Replaying packets is a replay attack, which IPsec anti-replay protects against.

questions.q: Ironman receives a packet with a digital signature from Thor. Which key does Ironman use to decrypt the signature?

choices.why: Ironman's private key decrypts data encrypted with Ironman's public key; it cannot decrypt a hash Thor signed.
Only the CA holds its private key; peers use the CA's public key to verify certificates.
Correct. The signature was encrypted with Thor's private key, so only Thor's public key decrypts it; Ironman then compares the hashes.
A PSK is a shared secret used for authentication; digital signatures rely on key pairs instead.

questions.q: Which set of methods can be used to access a CRL?

choices.why: Correct. CRLs can be accessed by LDAP, HTTP, or SCEP.
These are IPsec components for negotiation and packet protection, not ways to fetch a CRL.
These are management protocols for time, monitoring, and logging, not CRL distribution.
PGP and S/MIME encrypt email and SMTP carries it; none of them is used to retrieve CRLs.

questions.q: Which two hash algorithms were removed in TLS 1.3?

choices.why: SHA-256 and SHA-384 are strong hashes that remain in use; they are part of NGE.
SHA-3 and BLAKE2 are recommended modern hashes, not the ones TLS 1.3 removed.
Whirlpool and SHA-512 are 512-bit hashes considered strong; TLS 1.3 did not remove them for weakness.
Correct. TLS 1.3 removes MD5 and SHA-224, along with weak and less-used named elliptic curves.

questions.q: An analyst runs md5sum against three files with different names, and two of them show the same checksum. What does this indicate?

choices.text: The md5sum command failed on one file
choices.why: A matching checksum is a normal result, not an error; md5sum computes each file's hash independently.

choices.text: The two files were renamed copies of the same file name
choices.why: The filename is not part of the hash; the checksum reflects only the contents.

choices.text: The two files have the same contents
choices.why: Correct. Files with the same contents produce the same checksum even if their filenames differ.

choices.text: The two files are encrypted with the same key
choices.why: md5sum calculates a hash; it says nothing about encryption keys.

questions.q: Which statement about SCEP is accurate?

choices.text: It is an IETF open standard for revocation checking
choices.why: SCEP is not an open standard, and revocation status checking is done by CRLs or OCSP.

choices.text: It was developed by Cisco and automates certificate enrollment
choices.why: Correct. SCEP was developed by Cisco with other vendors to automate requesting and installing certificates; it is not an open standard.

choices.text: It is the format for storing public and private keys
choices.why: Storing public and private keys together is the role of PKCS #12.

choices.text: It defines the X.500 directory structure
choices.why: X.500 is the series of directory service standards; SCEP is an enrollment protocol.

questions.q: Which IPsec protection prevents an attacker from capturing valid packets and sending them again later?

choices.why: Nonrepudiation means the sender cannot deny sending the data; it does not stop replayed packets.
Correct. Anti-replay is the IPsec benefit that protects against replayed packets.
Perfect forward secrecy concerns protecting session keys if a long-term key is compromised, not detecting replayed packets.
NAT-T lets IPsec work through NAT devices using UDP 4500; it is not replay protection.

questions.q: After VPN users authenticate with certificates, the firewall reads the OU=sales field and assigns access rights stored in Active Directory. What is the main benefit of this design?

choices.text: It removes the need for a CA
choices.why: The certificates still have to be issued and signed by a CA; the OU field just maps users to rights.

choices.text: It encrypts the OU field with AES
choices.why: Certificate fields are signed by the CA, not encrypted; the benefit is centralized rights, not secrecy.

choices.text: It replaces the need for revocation checking
choices.why: Revocation checking with a CRL or OCSP is still needed; the OU field does not show whether a certificate is revoked.

choices.text: Rights are defined once in a directory and reused
choices.why: Correct. Using a certificate field such as OU=sales with Active Directory or another LDAP database lets you define access rights in one place and reuse them.

questions.q: Which group of algorithms is believed to be safe against quantum computing attacks?

choices.why: Correct. AES-256, SHA-384, and SHA-512 are believed to be post-quantum safe.
These classical public key algorithms rely on factoring and discrete logarithms, which quantum computers threaten.
These are already outdated or broken against classical attacks, let alone quantum ones.
These rely on discrete logarithm problems, which quantum computers threaten.

questions.q: Which cipher works like a substitution cipher but uses multiple alphabets and switches between them on a trigger character in the message?

choices.why: A transposition cipher rearranges letters rather than substituting them.
A stream cipher encrypts one bit at a time against a key stream; it does not switch alphabets on a trigger character.
Correct. A polyalphabetic cipher substitutes characters using multiple alphabets, switching between them on a trigger character.
A block cipher encrypts fixed-size blocks of bits, adding padding as needed.

questions.q: Which security goal ensures that a sender cannot later deny having sent the data?

choices.why: Confidentiality keeps data private through encryption; it does not prove who sent it.
Integrity confirms the data was not changed, typically by comparing hashes, but alone it does not bind the data to a sender.
Correct. Nonrepudiation means the sender cannot deny sending the data, which digital signatures provide.
Anti-replay is an IPsec protection against replayed packets, not proof of origin.

questions.q: In which attack does an attacker create a message that has a specific, chosen hash value?

choices.why: A collision attack finds or creates any two inputs that share the same hash, rather than matching one specific target hash.
A replay attack resends captured packets; it does not involve crafting a hash value.
A chosen-ciphertext attack targets encryption schemes (Kyber is IND-CCA2 secure against it), not hash values.
Correct. In a pre-image attack the attacker creates a message that produces a specific hash value.

questions.q: Remote users connect to an IPsec VPN from behind home routers that perform NAT. Which port must be allowed through the firewall for IPsec NAT Traversal?

choices.why: Correct. NAT-T encapsulates IPsec in UDP 4500 so it can pass through NAT devices.
UDP 500 is IKE (ISAKMP) key negotiation; NAT-T moves the traffic to UDP 4500.
TCP 389 is LDAP, used for directory lookups such as CRL retrieval.
IP protocol 51 is AH, which has no port and cannot be carried through NAT by NAT-T.

questions.q: What does a block cipher do when there is not enough plaintext to fill a block?

choices.why: Block ciphers do not switch to stream mode; they pad the final block.

choices.text: It adds padding to fill the block
choices.why: Correct. A block cipher adds padding when there is not enough data, which causes a very small amount of wasted overhead.
Discarding data would corrupt the message; the cipher pads the block instead.

choices.text: It encrypts the remainder with the public key
choices.why: Block ciphers are symmetric and do not use public keys; leftover space is filled with padding.

questions.q: An organization needs a fast, flexible hash for high-speed processing of large amounts of data with strong security, as an alternative to SHA-2 and MD5. Which algorithm fits?

choices.why: SHA-1 is a 160-bit hash that is outdated with known vulnerabilities, so its use is discouraged.
Whirlpool is a 512-bit attack-resistant hash, but the one described as fast and flexible for large data is BLAKE2.
HMAC-MD5 is a legacy keyed hash built on MD5; it is not the high-speed alternative described.
Correct. BLAKE2 is a fast, flexible hash for high-speed processing of large data with strong security, an alternative to SHA-2 and MD5.

questions.q: In IPsec, what is a pre-shared key (PSK) used for?

choices.why: Bulk data is encrypted with symmetric keys from a cipher such as AES; a PSK is used only for authentication.
Digests are produced by hash algorithms such as SHA-2; a PSK is not a hashing function.
Correct. A PSK is a shared secret used only for authentication, much like a password.
Certificates are signed by a CA using its private key, not with a PSK.

questions.q: Which item does a CA NOT put in the identity certificate it issues to a device?

choices.why: The device's public key is a core part of an identity certificate.
Correct. A private key is known only to the device that owns the key pair and is never shared, so it never appears in a certificate.
Certificates include a URL to check whether they have been revoked, the CRL location.
The CA assigns and tracks a serial number for each certificate it issues.

questions.q: Which PKCS standard is the CA's response to a PKCS #10 request, usually containing the identity certificate?

choices.why: Correct. PKCS #7 is the CA's response to a PKCS #10 request and usually holds the identity certificate.
PKCS #3 is the Diffie-Hellman key exchange standard.
PKCS #1 is the RSA cryptography standard.
PKCS #12 stores both public and private keys protected by a password-based key.

questions.q: Which NIST publication gives guidance for selecting, configuring, and using TLS?

choices.why: Correct. NIST SP 800-52 Rev. 2 provides guidance for selecting, configuring, and using TLS.
RFC 8446 defines the TLS 1.3 protocol itself; it is an IETF RFC, not NIST guidance.
PKCS #1 is the RSA cryptography standard, not TLS deployment guidance.
X.509v3 is the standard format for digital certificates, not guidance on configuring TLS.

questions.q: Which asymmetric encryption system is based on the Diffie-Hellman exchange?

choices.why: RSA is a separate asymmetric algorithm, mainly used today for digital signatures, and is not based on DH.
Correct. ElGamal is an asymmetric encryption system based on the DH exchange.
IDEA is a symmetric block cipher, not an asymmetric system.
Blowfish is a symmetric block cipher, not an asymmetric system.

questions.q: After two companies merge, each with its own CA, the engineers want clients of either CA to trust certificates signed by the other without building a new hierarchy. Which PKI topology should be used?

choices.why: A single root CA would mean replacing one of the CAs; it also has no fault tolerance.
A hierarchy requires a root CA signing subordinate CAs, which is a new vertical structure rather than trust between existing peers.
Correct. Cross-certification creates horizontal trust between two CAs so clients of either can trust the other's signatures.
Out-of-band verification checks a single certificate's hash by phone or another channel; it is not a topology.

questions.q: A security engineer wants to test the company's web server for known cryptographic weaknesses from a command-line tool. Which tool is described for this purpose?

choices.why: CyberChef is a web tool for operations such as XOR, Base64, AES, and hashing, not a server weakness scanner.
shasum prints SHA checksums of files; it does not test a web server's TLS setup.
verify md5 is a Cisco IOS command that checks a software image's integrity.
Correct. testssl.sh tests a web server for known cryptographic weaknesses.

questions.q: Classical public key algorithms are threatened by quantum computers because they rely on which mathematical problems?

choices.why: Module lattice problems are what post-quantum CRYSTALS algorithms rely on, because they resist quantum attacks.
Correct. Classical algorithms rely on integer factorization and discrete logarithms, which quantum computers threaten.
A sponge construction is how SHA-3 hashing works, not the basis of classical public key algorithms.
Multivariate polynomial-based math is one of the post-quantum construct families, not a classical basis.

questions.q: A malware analyst wants to tell other teams about a malicious file without risking anyone getting infected. What should the analyst share?

choices.why: Correct. Analysts share a malware file's hash instead of the file itself to avoid infection; Cisco Secure Malware Defense also uses malware hashes.

choices.text: The file encrypted with a PSK
choices.why: Sharing an encrypted copy still distributes the malware itself, which could infect someone once decrypted.
A malware file usually has no trustworthy certificate, and a certificate does not uniquely identify file contents the way a hash does.
Base64 is an encoding, not compression or protection; the shared content would still be the malware.

questions.q: What is the minimum symmetric key length considered fairly safe?

choices.why: 56 bits is far below the typical 112 to 256 bit range and is not considered safe.
64 bits is a common block size for older block ciphers, not a safe key length.
2048 bits is a typical asymmetric key length, not a symmetric minimum.
Correct. Symmetric keys are typically 112 to 256 bits, with 128 bits the minimum to be fairly safe.

questions.q: During a typical HTTPS session, how does the web server usually authenticate the user of the browser?

choices.why: The server usually does not authenticate the browser with a certificate; it relies on credentials instead.
PSKs are used for authenticating IPsec peers, not for browser users on HTTPS sites.
Correct. The server usually does not authenticate the browser cryptographically and uses a username and password instead.
OCSP reports a certificate's revocation status; it does not authenticate the user.

questions.q: Which kind of certificate identifies a client, such as a web server or router, and contains that host's public key?

choices.why: A root certificate identifies the CA itself and holds the CA's public key.
Cross-certification links two CAs horizontally; it does not identify an end host.
Correct. An identity certificate identifies a client such as a web server or router and contains its public key.
A subordinate CA certificate identifies an intermediate CA that issues identity certificates to clients.

questions.q: A router needs a certificate from a new CA. Which step must happen first?

choices.text: Authenticate the CA by getting its root certificate
choices.why: Correct. Step 1 is authenticating the CA, getting and trusting its root certificate, so the router has the CA public key to verify what the CA signs.

choices.text: Send an enrollment request with the public key
choices.why: Enrollment is step 2; without the CA's public key first, the router could not verify the certificate it gets back.
Installing the identity certificate is the last part of enrollment, after the CA signature has been verified.

choices.text: Download the CRL from the CA
choices.why: Revocation checking is used when authenticating peers; it is not the first step in obtaining a certificate.

questions.q: HTTPS combines HTTP with TLS/SSL. Which port does it use by default?

choices.why: TCP 80 is unencrypted HTTP; sites often redirect users from it to HTTPS.
Correct. HTTPS runs on TCP 443; the S stands for Secure.
TCP 389 is LDAP, used for directory lookups.
UDP 500 is IKE (ISAKMP) for IPsec key negotiation.

questions.q: Which hash algorithm uses a sponge construction and is the recommended SHA version?

choices.why: SHA-1 is a 160-bit outdated hash with known vulnerabilities; it does not use a sponge construction.
SHA-2 produces 224 to 512 bit digests but is not the version built on a sponge construction.
MD5 is a broken 128-bit hash that should be avoided.
Correct. SHA-3 uses a sponge construction, supports sequential, parallel, and tree modes, and is the recommended SHA version.

questions.q: In cryptography, what is a cipher?

choices.text: The encrypted output of an algorithm
choices.why: The encrypted output is called ciphertext, not the cipher.

choices.text: A secret value shared between peers
choices.why: A secret value that tells the algorithm how to encrypt is the key; a shared secret for authentication is a PSK.
A fixed-length summary of data is a hash or digest.

choices.text: A set of rules for performing encryption or decryption
choices.why: Correct. A cipher is an algorithm, a set of rules for how to perform encryption or decryption.

questions.q: Why are asymmetric algorithms used only for infrequent tasks such as authenticating a VPN peer and generating keying material?

choices.text: They have a high CPU cost
choices.why: Correct. Asymmetric algorithms are more secure but need much more CPU, so they are used sparingly rather than for bulk data.
Asymmetric algorithms such as RSA are the main method for authentication with digital signatures.

choices.text: They require padding for every packet
choices.why: Padding is a property of block ciphers, which are symmetric; it is not why asymmetric algorithms are used sparingly.

choices.text: They use the same key on both peers
choices.why: Using the same key on both sides describes symmetric algorithms; asymmetric algorithms use a public and private key pair.

questions.q: Why are hash collisions possible even with a strong hash function?

choices.text: Hash functions use a public key
choices.why: Hash functions do not use public keys; a keyed hash uses a secret key and is called HMAC.

choices.text: Inputs are unlimited in length but outputs are fixed
choices.why: Correct. Because there are unlimited possible inputs and a fixed number of outputs, two different inputs can produce the same hash.
The same data always produces the same hash; that consistency is what makes hashes useful for integrity checks.
Cryptographic hash functions are one-way; they cannot be reversed to recover the input.

questions.q: Which asymmetric algorithm was developed by the U.S. National Security Agency?

choices.why: RSA is named for Rivest, Shamir, and Adleman, its inventors, not the NSA.
Diffie-Hellman is a key exchange algorithm named for its inventors, not developed by the NSA.
Correct. The Digital Signature Algorithm (DSA) was developed by the U.S. National Security Agency.
AES is a symmetric block cipher, not an asymmetric algorithm.

questions.q: Which hash algorithm produces a 512-bit digest and is described as resistant to various attacks?

choices.why: Correct. Whirlpool is a 512-bit hash resistant to various attacks.
MD5 produces a 128-bit hash and is broken.
SHA-1 produces a 160-bit hash and is outdated.
HMAC-SHA-1 is a keyed hash built on 160-bit SHA-1, not a 512-bit algorithm.

questions.q: A firewall rule must permit IPsec AH traffic. Which value should the rule match?

choices.why: IP protocol 50 is ESP, the IPsec method that provides encryption.
AH has no port number; it is identified by IP protocol 51.
UDP 4500 is used by NAT Traversal for IPsec through NAT.
Correct. AH is IP protocol 51 and has no port.

questions.q: What is a certificate's thumbprint (fingerprint)?

choices.text: The CA's digital signature on the certificate
choices.why: The CA's signature is a separate field; the thumbprint is a hash of the certificate.

choices.text: The serial number assigned by the CA
choices.why: The serial number uniquely identifies the certificate, but the thumbprint is a hash of it.
Correct. The thumbprint is the hash of the certificate, and the thumbprint algorithm is the hash algorithm used.

choices.text: The public key of the subject
choices.why: The public key field holds the subject's key; the thumbprint is calculated over the whole certificate.

questions.q: Thor wants to send Ironman an encrypted email using PGP so that only Ironman can read it. Which key does Thor use to encrypt the message?

choices.why: Encrypting with Thor's private key creates a signature anyone with Thor's public key can read, so it provides no confidentiality.
Correct. Thor encrypts with Ironman's public key, and only Ironman's private key can decrypt it.
Ironman's private key is known only to Ironman and is never shared, so Thor cannot use it.
The CA's public key is used to verify certificates the CA signed, not to encrypt email for a person.

questions.q: Which port does LDAP, a common protocol for directory lookups and CRL retrieval, use?

choices.why: Correct. LDAP uses TCP/UDP 389, and CRLs can be fetched over LDAP or HTTP.
TCP 443 is HTTPS, HTTP combined with TLS/SSL.
UDP 123 is NTP, which keeps time accurate.
TCP 49 is TACACS+, an AAA protocol, not LDAP.

questions.q: Which hash algorithm is required for classified information of higher importance under NGE guidance?

choices.why: SHA-256 is adequate for sensitive information, but classified information of higher importance requires SHA-384.
SHA-1 is outdated with known vulnerabilities and is not used for classified information.
MD5 is broken and NIST no longer recommends it for any cryptographic use.
Correct. SHA-384 is required for classified information of higher importance.

questions.q: Which elliptic curves does next-generation encryption use?

choices.why: These are not the NGE curves; NGE specifies P-256 and P-384.
Correct. NGE uses the P-256 and P-384 elliptic curves.
These are not the curves named for NGE; NGE uses P-256 and P-384.
224 and 2048 are a hash size and a common RSA key length, not the NGE curves.

questions.q: Which certificate revocation checking method is rarely used in PKI because it is proprietary?

choices.why: CRLs are the primary and most popular revocation method, not a rarely used one.
OCSP is the common alternative to CRLs that checks a single certificate; it is not proprietary.
Correct. Cisco AAA can validate certificates and check revocation, but it is proprietary and rarely used in PKI.
LDAP is a transport that can deliver CRLs; it is not a separate proprietary revocation method.

questions.q: A company with tens of thousands of clients runs a PKI with only a single root CA. Which problem is most likely?

choices.text: Clients cannot verify the root's signature
choices.why: Clients can verify the root once they have its certificate; the issue with one CA is load and resilience.
Every CA assigns serial numbers regardless of topology.

choices.text: Cross-certification is required for every client
choices.why: Cross-certification links two CAs; it is not required for clients of a single CA.

choices.text: The CA may be overloaded and has no fault tolerance
choices.why: Correct. A single root CA can be overloaded by many clients and has no fault tolerance; publishing CRLs elsewhere only offloads some work.

questions.q: Which PKCS standard covers Diffie-Hellman key exchange?

choices.why: Correct. PKCS #3 is the Diffie-Hellman key exchange standard.
PKCS #1 is the RSA cryptography standard.
PKCS #7 is the CA's response to a certificate request.
PKCS #10 is the certificate request sent to a CA.

questions.q: Both CRYSTALS algorithms, Kyber and Dilithium, rely on which type of mathematical problem?

choices.why: Integer factorization is what classical RSA relies on, and quantum computers threaten it.
Elliptic curve discrete logarithms underlie ECDSA and ECDH, which are classical algorithms.
Correct. Kyber and Dilithium both rely on module lattice problems.
Code-based math is another post-quantum family, used by algorithms such as Classic McEliece, not CRYSTALS.

questions.q: When IPsec peers are configured to authenticate each other with digital signatures, which configuration term is used?

choices.why: pre-share is the term for authenticating with a pre-shared key, not digital signatures.
rsa-encr refers to RSA encrypted nonces, a different authentication method; digital signature authentication uses rsa-signatures.
A crypto map ties IPsec policy to an interface; it is not the term for an authentication method.
Correct. rsa-signatures is the configuration term used when IPsec peers authenticate with digital signatures.

questions.q: What is the role of IKE in IPsec?

choices.why: Packet encryption is done by ESP using a symmetric cipher such as AES; IKE handles negotiation.

choices.text: It performs much of the negotiation and management IPsec needs
choices.why: Correct. IKE does much of the negotiation and key management that IPsec requires.

choices.text: It issues identity certificates to VPN peers
choices.why: Identity certificates are issued and signed by a CA, not by IKE.
That describes AH, the IPsec method without encryption.

questions.q: Which certificate field states what the public key may be used for?

choices.why: Correct. The key usage field defines what the certificate's public key may be used for.
The subject field identifies the person or entity the certificate belongs to.
The signature algorithm field names the algorithm the CA used to sign the certificate.
The issuer field names the CA that created and issued the certificate.

questions.q: A company wants to offer encrypted access to a customer portal. Why is SSL/TLS a better fit than IPsec for this?

choices.why: IPsec can encrypt any IP traffic at Layer 3, including web traffic; the barrier is client requirements.
TLS servers do use certificates; the browser verifies the server's certificate.

choices.text: Not every customer has an IPsec client, certificate, or PSK
choices.why: Correct. Not everyone has an IPsec client, a digital certificate, or a PSK, while almost every browser supports SSL/TLS.

choices.text: IPsec only works for remote-access VPNs
choices.why: IPsec is used for both remote-access and site-to-site VPNs.

questions.q: Which change did TLS 1.3 make to cipher suites?

choices.text: It added MD5 for backward compatibility
choices.why: TLS 1.3 removed MD5 rather than adding it.

choices.text: It added more named elliptic curves
choices.why: TLS 1.3 removed weak and less-used named elliptic curves.

choices.text: It made RSA mandatory for bulk encryption
choices.why: Bulk encryption is done with symmetric ciphers, not RSA, and TLS 1.3 made no such change.

choices.text: It separated key agreement and authentication from the cipher suites
choices.why: Correct. TLS 1.3 separates key agreement and authentication algorithms from the cipher suites.

questions.q: Which activities make up key management?

choices.text: Generating, verifying, exchanging, storing, and destroying keys
choices.why: Correct. Key management covers the whole key lifecycle, from generating and verifying keys to exchanging, storing, and destroying them at the end of their lifetime.
These describe how digital signatures are created and checked, not the handling of keys over their lifetime.
These describe how a block cipher processes data, not the lifecycle of keys.
These are CA and PKI certificate operations; key management is about the keys themselves.

questions.q: Why is MD5 no longer considered secure?

choices.text: Its 512-bit output is too slow to compute
choices.why: MD5 produces a 128-bit hash, and speed is not the problem; it is broken by collisions.

choices.text: It requires a secret key that is easily stolen
choices.why: MD5 is an unkeyed hash; adding a key makes an HMAC such as HMAC-MD5.

choices.text: It is vulnerable to collision and pre-image attacks
choices.why: Correct. MD5 is a simple algorithm that modern computing can break, it is vulnerable to collisions and pre-image attacks, and NIST no longer recommends it for any cryptographic use.

choices.text: It can only hash files smaller than 16 bytes
choices.why: MD5 accepts input of any length; its output is 16 bytes, not its input limit.

questions.q: A sender hashes a packet and attaches the hash. In transit, one bit of the packet is changed. What happens at the receiver?

choices.text: The hashes still match because only one bit changed
choices.why: A single changed bit produces a different hash, which is exactly what makes hashing an integrity check.

choices.text: The hash the receiver calculates will not match the attached hash
choices.why: Correct. The receiver hashes the packet again and compares; if even one bit changed, the hashes will not match.

choices.text: The receiver decrypts the hash to recover the original bit
choices.why: Hashes are one-way and cannot be decrypted to recover data.

choices.text: The receiver requests a new key from the CA
choices.why: A failed integrity check does not trigger a CA key request; the packet is simply seen as altered.

questions.q: At which OSI layer does IPsec protect packets?

choices.why: Layer 2 protection would operate on frames, not IP packets; IPsec works at Layer 3.
IPsec is not a transport layer protocol; it protects IP packets at Layer 3.
Layer 7 is the application layer, where protocols such as HTTP run; IPsec protects IP packets at Layer 3.
Correct. IPsec is a suite of protocols and algorithms that protects IP packets at Layer 3.

questions.q: What is a subordinate (intermediate) CA?

choices.text: A CA that has been revoked by the root
choices.why: Subordinate CAs can be invalidated, but being revoked is not what defines them.

choices.text: A CA that trusts another CA horizontally
choices.why: Horizontal trust between two CAs is cross-certification.

choices.text: A CA that the root CA delegates to issue identity certificates
choices.why: Correct. A subordinate CA receives authority from the root CA to issue identity certificates to clients.

choices.text: A CA built into every web browser
choices.why: Browsers ship with root certificates of mainstream CAs; that does not define a subordinate CA.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT one of the goals of cryptography listed in the chapter?

choices.why: Correct. The listed goals are data confidentiality, data integrity, authentication, and nonrepudiation; availability is not one of them.
Data confidentiality, achieved through encryption, is one of the goals of cryptography.
Authentication, verifying a peer's identity, is one of the goals of cryptography.
Nonrepudiation, preventing a sender from denying sending data, is one of the goals of cryptography.

questions.q: Which PKCS standard is the RSA cryptography standard?

choices.why: PKCS #3 is the Diffie-Hellman key exchange standard.
PKCS #12 stores both public and private keys protected by a password-based key.
PKCS #10 is the certificate request sent to a CA.
Correct. RSA is also called PKCS #1, the RSA cryptography standard.

questions.q: A user visiting an internal site gets a browser pop-up saying the certificate is not trusted. What is the recommended guidance for users?

choices.text: Accept it if the URL looks correct
choices.why: A correct-looking URL does not prove the server's identity; an untrusted certificate could belong to an attacker.
Correct. Users should be trained never to accept an untrusted certificate, because the browser could not verify the CA's signature.

choices.text: Accept it once and then clear the cache
choices.why: Clearing the cache does not undo the risk of connecting to an unverified server.

choices.text: Switch from HTTPS to HTTP and retry
choices.why: HTTP on TCP 80 is unencrypted, which removes protection instead of solving the trust problem.

questions.q: A university wants laptops to authenticate to the wireless network at the network edge using digital certificates. Which technology provides this?

choices.why: NAT-T carries IPsec through NAT on UDP 4500; it is not network edge authentication.
OCSP checks a certificate's revocation status; it does not control network access by itself.
Correct. 802.1X provides network edge authentication, such as wireless access for PCs and users, and can use digital certificates.
S/MIME uses key pairs to encrypt email, not to authenticate devices to a wireless network.

questions.q: According to NIST SP 800-52 Rev. 2, what must the CA that issues TLS server certificates do?

choices.text: Publish revocation information in OCSP responses
choices.why: Correct. Certificates must come from a CA that publishes revocation information in OCSP responses; the CA may also publish a CRL.

choices.text: Issue only PKCS #12 files to servers
choices.why: PKCS #12 is a key storage format; SP 800-52 Rev. 2 does not limit CAs to it.

choices.text: Use only a single server certificate per server
choices.why: SP 800-52 Rev. 2 notes that multiple server certificates support algorithm and key size agility.

choices.text: Be cross-certified with every public CA
choices.why: Cross-certification is an optional PKI topology, not a requirement of SP 800-52 Rev. 2.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT one of the mathematical construct families used for post-quantum algorithms?

choices.why: Lattice-based math is a post-quantum family; CRYSTALS Kyber and Dilithium use module lattices.
Code-based math is one of the post-quantum construct families.
Hash-based math is one of the post-quantum construct families.
Correct. Integer factorization is what classical algorithms such as RSA rely on, and quantum computers threaten it.

questions.q: The NIST post-quantum standardization competition has three tracks. Which set lists them?

choices.text: Hashing, block ciphers, and stream ciphers
choices.why: These are classical symmetric and hashing categories, not the NIST post-quantum tracks.

choices.text: Key-establishment, digital signature, and public-key encryption
choices.why: Correct. The three tracks are key-establishment, digital signature, and public-key encryption algorithms.
These are PKI certificate lifecycle tasks, not post-quantum algorithm tracks.
This is the CIA triad of security goals, not the NIST competition tracks.

questions.q: An analyst needs a single web tool to Base64-decode a string, XOR some data, compute hashes, and parse an X.509 certificate. Which tool fits?

choices.why: testssl.sh tests a web server for known cryptographic weaknesses; it is not a general data transformation tool.
checktls.com tests a website's TLS setup rather than decoding and transforming arbitrary data.
Correct. CyberChef is a web tool for XOR, Base64, AES, hashes, checksums, hexdumps, compression, IPv6 and X.509 parsing, and character encoding.
keybase.io is a public PGP key server, used to publish and find public keys.

questions.q: How many hexadecimal digits are used to display a SHA-512 hash?

choices.why: 32 hex digits represent 128 bits, the size of an MD5 hash.
40 hex digits represent 160 bits, the size of a SHA-1 hash.
64 hex digits represent 256 bits, such as SHA-256.
Correct. SHA-512 is 512 bits, shown as 128 hex digits.

questions.q: What is the widely accepted standard for digital certificates?

choices.why: Correct. X.509 Version 3 is the widely accepted standard for digital certificates and uses X.500 naming.
X.500 is a series of directory service standards; X.509v3 borrows its naming but X.500 is not the certificate standard.
PKCS #10 is the format for certificate requests, not the certificate standard itself.
RFC 8446 defines TLS 1.3, not the digital certificate format.

questions.q: In the X.500 naming used by certificates, what does CN=Thor represent?

choices.why: The organizational unit is OU, such as OU=engineering.
The organization is O, such as O=cisco.com.
Correct. CN is the common name, such as CN=Thor.
The country is C in the subject field, not CN.

questions.q: Which statement about a private key is true?

choices.text: It is known only to the device that owns the key pair
choices.why: Correct. The private key is never shared; only the owning device knows it.

choices.text: It is included in the device's identity certificate
choices.why: An identity certificate carries the public key; the private key is never put in a certificate.

choices.text: It is published to a public key server
choices.why: Public key servers such as pgp.mit.edu publish public keys, not private keys.

choices.text: It is the same key on both VPN peers
choices.why: Sharing the same key on both peers describes symmetric encryption, not a private key.

questions.q: Two VPN peers exchange their symmetric encryption keys in plaintext across the internet. What is the result if an eavesdropper captures them?

choices.why: With the keys, the attacker can decrypt the traffic, so the main loss is confidentiality.

choices.text: The attacker can decrypt the traffic and confidentiality is lost
choices.why: Correct. If keys are sent in plaintext, an eavesdropper can decrypt the traffic, which is why key management and DH key exchange matter.

choices.text: Nothing, because the data is still hashed
choices.why: Hashing protects integrity, not confidentiality; the captured keys still decrypt the data.

choices.text: The CA automatically revokes the keys
choices.why: The CA is not involved in symmetric keys exchanged between peers and would not detect the capture.

questions.q: In a PKI that uses RSA digital signatures between two VPN peers, why does each peer need its own key pair?

choices.text: Because DH requires two private keys per peer
choices.why: DH negotiates shared keying material; the per-peer key pairs here are for signature authentication.

choices.text: Because each key pair can sign only one packet
choices.why: A key pair can sign many packets; it is not single-use like a one-time pad.

choices.text: Because the CA keeps one copy of each private key
choices.why: The CA never holds clients' private keys; it signs certificates containing their public keys.

choices.text: Because both sides authenticate each other
choices.why: Correct. Each party has its own key pair because both sides authenticate each other, usually in both directions in an IPsec VPN.

questions.q: Which AES mode of operation is part of next-generation encryption (NGE)?

choices.why: Electronic codebook is not the AES mode listed in NGE; NGE uses Galois/Counter Mode.
Cipher block chaining is an older mode and is not the NGE mode, which is GCM.
Correct. AES in Galois/Counter Mode (GCM) is the AES mode used in NGE.
Cipher feedback mode is not the mode named for NGE; NGE uses AES-GCM.
